Question: Let \(S\) be a subset of \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 30\}\) with the property that no pair of distinct elements in \(S\) has a sum divisible by \(5.\) What is the largest possible size of \(S?\)
Solution:
Whether a sum is divisible by \(5\) depends only on the two numbers' remainders after division by \(5\). Among \(1,2,\ldots,30\), each of the five possible remainders \(0,1,2,3,4\) occurs six times.

Any number with remainder \(1\) forms a forbidden sum with any number with remainder \(4\). Thus \(S\) cannot contain numbers from both of those classes, and it contains at most six numbers from their union. Likewise, the remainder-\(2\) and remainder-\(3\) classes together contribute at most six numbers.

Finally, any two distinct multiples of \(5\) have a sum divisible by \(5\), so at most one multiple of \(5\) can be included. These three groups partition all thirty numbers, giving the universal bound
\[
|S|\le6+6+1=13.
\]
To attain it, take all six numbers with remainder \(1\), all six with remainder \(2\), and the number \(5\). A pair from the first two classes has sum remainder \(2\), \(3\), or \(4\). Pairing \(5\) with any other selected number gives remainder \(1\) or \(2\). Since there is only one selected multiple of \(5\), every pair of distinct selected numbers is allowed.

Therefore the largest possible size is \(\boxed{13}\), choice B.
